core_themes.name: Overfishing and EU sustainability obligations
core_themes.claim: Stock assessments and landing trends show lobster and crawfish stocks in English waters are being overfished, threatening the UK's ability to meet MSY obligations under the CFP and MSFD by 2020.

core_themes.name: Market failure from removing berried females
core_themes.claim: Fishing is a common-good problem and landing berried lobsters/crawfish imposes a particularly large external cost because it removes eggs that would otherwise replenish the stock, worsening over-exploitation.

core_themes.name: Inconsistent and unevaluated local bans
core_themes.claim: Existing IFCA inshore bans on landing berried lobsters/crawfish are patchy, unassessed for effectiveness, and create enforcement difficulties because stocks and vessels extend beyond IFCA district boundaries.

core_themes.name: Choice of national ban over alternatives
core_themes.claim: A national ban via secondary legislation is preferred over doing nothing, relying on voluntary v-notching (which has seen insufficient uptake since 2000), or extending IFCA byelaws (which cannot cover stocks and vessels operating beyond 6nm), because only a national ban gives sufficient spatial coverage and resolves cross-boundary enforcement problems.

core_themes.name: Modelled stock and landings benefits
core_themes.claim: Cefas population modelling indicates that a ban on landing berried lobsters will increase spawning stock biomass and ultimately landings (3-43% higher after 15 years depending on exploitation rate), justifying the policy despite short-term costs.

core_themes.name: Business costs versus long-term gains
core_themes.claim: The ban imposes quantifiable costs on fishers and government (lost revenue, familiarisation and enforcement costs, totalling an Equivalent Annual Net Cost to Business of £2.29m) that are presented as justified by uncertain but expected longer-term revenue gains from stock recovery.

core_themes.name: Legislative vehicle and scope of the ban
core_themes.claim: The ban will be implemented by amending the existing Statutory Instrument that prohibits landing v-notched lobsters/crawfish, applying it to all relevant British and Scottish vessels fishing in English waters (0-200nm) while excluding foreign vessels because their landings are negligible.

core_themes.name: Enforcement mechanism and costs
core_themes.claim: The MMO and IFCAs will enforce the ban by investing in testing kits and training to detect scrubbed eggs, integrated into routine inspection activity at an estimated annual cost, with no additional enforcement costs expected.

core_themes.name: Further testing of assumptions through consultation
core_themes.claim: Key assumptions underlying the policy's design and modelling (e.g. vessel behaviour, compliance, effectiveness of local bans) remain undecided and will be tested and refined through a formal consultation and stakeholder workshops before final implementation.
